# 1. Environment and Libraries

This project presents an end-to-end data science analysis of the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist. The workflow covers data acquisition, data understanding, data preprocessing, exploratory data analysis, statistical hypothesis testing, customer segmentation, and predictive modeling.

## 1.1 Install and Load Libraries
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(tibble)
```


```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
required_packages <- c(
  "tidyverse", "lubridate", "janitor", "skimr",
  "naniar", "GGally", "broom", "scales",
  "tidymodels", "ranger", "isotree"
)

new_packages <- required_packages[
  !required_packages %in% rownames(installed.packages())
]

set.seed(1)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

options(
  scipen = 999,
  dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE
)
```

# 2. Data Acquisition

The dataset can be obtained from Kaggle. This section uses the Kaggle CLI to download the dataset automatically.

Make sure that the Kaggle CLI is installed and your Kaggle API credentials are configured. Alternatively, download the dataset manually and place all CSV files inside the `data` directory.

```{r data-acquisition, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
csv_files <- list.files(
  "C:/Users/Users/Downloads/olist_data",
  pattern = "\\.csv$",
  full.names = TRUE
)

if (length(csv_files) == 0) {
  stop("No CSV files were found in the data directory.")
}

data_list <- setNames(
  lapply(csv_files, readr::read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE),
  tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(csv_files))
)

names(data_list)
```

## 2.1 Load Individual Tables

```{r load-tables}
orders <- data_list[["olist_orders_dataset"]]
customers <- data_list[["olist_customers_dataset"]]
order_items <- data_list[["olist_order_items_dataset"]]
products <- data_list[["olist_products_dataset"]]
sellers <- data_list[["olist_sellers_dataset"]]
payments <- data_list[["olist_order_payments_dataset"]]
reviews <- data_list[["olist_order_reviews_dataset"]]
categories <- data_list[["product_category_name_translation"]]

required_tables <- c(
  "orders", "customers", "order_items", "products",
  "sellers", "payments", "reviews", "categories"
)

missing_tables <- required_tables[
  !vapply(required_tables, function(x) !is.null(get(x)), logical(1))
]

if (length(missing_tables) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Missing required datasets: ",
    paste(missing_tables, collapse = ", ")
  )
}

rm(data_list, csv_files, required_tables, missing_tables)
```

# 3. Data Understanding and Quality Assessment

## 3.1 Dataset Overview

The Olist dataset consists of multiple relational tables. Each table has a different level of granularity, which must be considered before joining the data.

```{r dataset-overview}
dataset_overview <- tibble(
  dataset = c(
    "orders", "customers", "order_items", "products",
    "sellers", "payments", "reviews", "categories"
  ),
  rows = c(
    nrow(orders), nrow(customers), nrow(order_items),
    nrow(products), nrow(sellers), nrow(payments),
    nrow(reviews), nrow(categories)
  ),
  columns = c(
    ncol(orders), ncol(customers), ncol(order_items),
    ncol(products), ncol(sellers), ncol(payments),
    ncol(reviews), ncol(categories)
  )
)

knitr::kable(dataset_overview)
```

## 3.2 Data Structure

The structure of each dataset is inspected to identify variable types, column names, and potential inconsistencies.

```{r data-structure}
glimpse(orders)
glimpse(order_items)
glimpse(customers)
glimpse(products)
```

## 3.3 Missing Value Assessment

Missing values are evaluated to understand the completeness of each variable and identify columns that may require additional preprocessing.

```{r missing-values}
missing_summary <- function(data) {
  tibble(
    column = names(data),
    missing_count = vapply(
      data,
      function(x) sum(is.na(x)),
      integer(1)
    ),
    missing_percentage = vapply(
      data,
      function(x) mean(is.na(x)) * 100,
      numeric(1)
    )
  ) |>
    arrange(desc(missing_percentage))
}

missing_summary(orders)
```

```{r missing-visualization, fig.height=5}
naniar::vis_miss(orders)
```

## 3.4 Duplicate Assessment

Duplicate records are examined across the main datasets. Duplicate counts should be interpreted in the context of each table's structure.

```{r duplicate-assessment}
duplicate_summary <- tibble(
  dataset = c(
    "orders", "customers", "order_items",
    "products", "sellers", "payments", "reviews"
  ),
  duplicate_rows = c(
    sum(duplicated(orders)),
    sum(duplicated(customers)),
    sum(duplicated(order_items)),
    sum(duplicated(products)),
    sum(duplicated(sellers)),
    sum(duplicated(payments)),
    sum(duplicated(reviews))
  )
)

knitr::kable(duplicate_summary)
```

## 3.5 Relational Structure

The main relationships between the datasets are:

- `orders` serves as the central transaction table.
- `customers` is linked through `customer_id`.
- `order_items` is linked through `order_id`.
- `products` and `sellers` are connected through `order_items`.
- `payments` and `reviews` are also linked through `order_id`.

A single order may contain multiple items, payment records, or review records. Joining these tables directly may multiply rows. Therefore, the relevant tables should be aggregated before constructing an order-level analytical dataset.

# 4. Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering

## 4.1 Datetime Conversion

Timestamp columns are converted into datetime objects to support temporal calculations and feature extraction.

```{r datetime-conversion}
datetime_columns <- c(
  "order_purchase_timestamp",
  "order_approved_at",
  "order_delivered_carrier_date",
  "order_delivered_customer_date",
  "order_estimated_delivery_date"
)

orders <- orders |>
  mutate(
    across(
      all_of(datetime_columns),
      ~ lubridate::ymd_hms(.x, quiet = TRUE)
    )
  )
```

## 4.2 Order-Level Aggregation

### Item Aggregation

Item-level records are aggregated to produce one row per order.

```{r item-aggregation}
item_summary <- order_items |>
  group_by(order_id) |>
  summarise(
    item_count = n(),
    total_price = sum(price, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_freight = sum(freight_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_freight = mean(freight_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### Payment Aggregation

Payment records are aggregated to avoid duplicating orders during the merge process.

```{r payment-aggregation}
payment_summary <- payments |>
  group_by(order_id) |>
  summarise(
    payment_value = sum(payment_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    payment_installments = max(
      payment_installments,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    payment_types = n_distinct(payment_type),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### Review Aggregation

```{r review-aggregation}
review_summary <- reviews |>
  group_by(order_id) |>
  summarise(
    review_score = mean(review_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### Customer Information

The unique customer identifier is retained for the subsequent RFM analysis.

```{r customer-information}
customer_summary <- customers |>
  select(
    customer_id,
    customer_unique_id,
    customer_city,
    customer_state
  )
```

### Merge Order-Level Data

```{r merge-order-data}
order_level <- orders |>
  left_join(item_summary, by = "order_id") |>
  left_join(payment_summary, by = "order_id") |>
  left_join(review_summary, by = "order_id") |>
  left_join(customer_summary, by = "customer_id")

dim(order_level)
head(order_level)
```

## 4.3 Delivery and Transaction Features

Several temporal variables are engineered to measure order processing and delivery performance.

```{r delivery-features}
order_level <- order_level |>
  mutate(
    approval_duration = as.numeric(
      difftime(
        order_approved_at,
        order_purchase_timestamp,
        units = "days"
      )
    ),
    delivery_duration = as.numeric(
      difftime(
        order_delivered_customer_date,
        order_purchase_timestamp,
        units = "days"
      )
    ),
    shipping_duration = as.numeric(
      difftime(
        order_delivered_customer_date,
        order_delivered_carrier_date,
        units = "days"
      )
    ),
    estimated_delivery_duration = as.numeric(
      difftime(
        order_estimated_delivery_date,
        order_purchase_timestamp,
        units = "days"
      )
    ),
    delivery_delay = as.numeric(
      difftime(
        order_delivered_customer_date,
        order_estimated_delivery_date,
        units = "days"
      )
    )
  )
```

### Calendar Features

```{r calendar-features}
order_level <- order_level |>
  mutate(
    purchase_year = year(order_purchase_timestamp),
    purchase_month = month(
      order_purchase_timestamp,
      label = TRUE,
      abbr = TRUE
    ),
    purchase_day = day(order_purchase_timestamp),
    purchase_weekday = wday(
      order_purchase_timestamp,
      label = TRUE
    ),
    purchase_hour = hour(order_purchase_timestamp),
    is_weekend = wday(order_purchase_timestamp) %in% c(1, 7)
  )
```

## 4.4 Product Characteristics

Product dimensions and weight are aggregated at the order level to provide additional information about shipment characteristics.

```{r product-features}
product_summary <- order_items |>
  left_join(
    products |>
      select(
        product_id,
        product_category_name,
        product_weight_g,
        product_length_cm,
        product_height_cm,
        product_width_cm
      ),
    by = "product_id"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    product_volume_cm3 =
      product_length_cm *
      product_height_cm *
      product_width_cm
  ) |>
  group_by(order_id) |>
  summarise(
    avg_product_weight = mean(product_weight_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_product_volume = mean(product_volume_cm3, na.rm = TRUE),
    product_categories = n_distinct(product_category_name),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

order_level <- order_level |>
  left_join(product_summary, by = "order_id")
```

## 4.5 Outlier Screening

Isolation Forest is used to identify observations with unusual patterns. Identified outliers are not automatically removed because extreme values may represent valid transactions.

```{r outlier-screening, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
outlier_features <- order_level |>
  select(
    total_price,
    total_freight,
    item_count,
    delivery_duration
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ replace_na(.x, median(.x, na.rm = TRUE))
    )
  )

outlier_model <- isotree::isolation.forest(
  outlier_features,
  ntrees = 100,
  sample_size = min(256, nrow(outlier_features)),
  seed = 42
)

order_level$outlier_score <- predict(
  outlier_model,
  outlier_features,
  type = "score"
)

summary(order_level$outlier_score)
```

# 5. Exploratory Data Analysis

## 5.1 Descriptive Statistics

Descriptive statistics are used to examine the central tendency, dispersion, and distribution of important numerical variables.

```{r descriptive-statistics}
order_level |>
  select(
    total_price,
    total_freight,
    item_count,
    delivery_duration,
    approval_duration,
    shipping_duration
  ) |>
  summary()
```

## 5.2 Distribution of Numerical Variables

```{r numerical-distribution, fig.height=7}
order_level |>
  select(
    total_price,
    total_freight,
    delivery_duration,
    approval_duration
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 40,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Numerical Variables",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Frequency"
  )
```

## 5.3 Correlation Analysis

Correlation analysis is performed to examine linear associations among numerical variables. Correlation does not imply causation.

```{r correlation-analysis, fig.height=6}
correlation_data <- order_level |>
  select(
    total_price,
    total_freight,
    item_count,
    delivery_duration,
    approval_duration,
    shipping_duration,
    estimated_delivery_duration
  )

GGally::ggcorr(
  correlation_data,
  label = TRUE,
  label_round = 2,
  label_size = 3
)
```

## 5.4 Monthly Order Volume and Delivery Duration

Monthly aggregation is used to examine changes in transaction activity and delivery performance over time.

```{r monthly-analysis}
monthly_analysis <- order_level |>
  filter(!is.na(order_purchase_timestamp)) |>
  mutate(
    purchase_month = floor_date(
      order_purchase_timestamp,
      unit = "month"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(purchase_month) |>
  summarise(
    order_volume = n_distinct(order_id),
    avg_delivery_duration = mean(
      delivery_duration,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(head(monthly_analysis, 12))
```

### Monthly Order Volume

```{r monthly-order-volume, fig.height=5}
ggplot(
  monthly_analysis,
  aes(purchase_month, order_volume)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly Order Volume",
    x = "Purchase Month",
    y = "Number of Orders"
  )
```

### Average Delivery Duration

```{r monthly-delivery-duration, fig.height=5}
ggplot(
  monthly_analysis,
  aes(purchase_month, avg_delivery_duration)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, color = "darkorange") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Delivery Duration Over Time",
    x = "Purchase Month",
    y = "Average Delivery Duration (Days)"
  )
```

Interpretation: These visualizations provide an overview of transaction activity and delivery performance over time. Similar movements between order volume and delivery duration do not establish a causal relationship. Other factors, such as seasonal demand, logistics capacity, and customer location, may also influence delivery performance.

## 5.5 Order Status Analysis

```{r order-status}
order_level |>
  group_by(order_status) |>
  summarise(
    total_orders = n_distinct(order_id),
    avg_delivery_days = mean(delivery_duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_delivery_days = median(delivery_duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_orders)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## 5.6 Hypothesis Testing: Weekday vs Weekend

The objective is to determine whether delivery duration distributions differ between orders purchased on weekdays and weekends.

Hypotheses:

- H0: The delivery duration distributions are equal between weekdays and weekends.
- H1: The delivery duration distributions differ between weekdays and weekends.

The Mann-Whitney U test is used because it does not require normally distributed observations.

```{r mann-whitney-test}
test_data <- order_level |>
  filter(
    !is.na(delivery_duration),
    delivery_duration >= 0
  )

weekday_group <- test_data |>
  filter(!is_weekend) |>
  pull(delivery_duration)

weekend_group <- test_data |>
  filter(is_weekend) |>
  pull(delivery_duration)

mann_whitney_result <- wilcox.test(
  weekday_group,
  weekend_group,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  exact = FALSE
)

mann_whitney_result
```

### Statistical Decision

```{r hypothesis-interpretation}
alpha <- 0.05
p_value <- mann_whitney_result$p.value

if (p_value < alpha) {
  cat(
    "Decision: Reject H0. There is sufficient statistical evidence ",
    "that delivery duration distributions differ between weekdays and weekends."
  )
} else {
  cat(
    "Decision: Fail to reject H0. There is insufficient statistical evidence ",
    "to conclude that delivery duration distributions differ."
  )
}
```

## 5.7 Customer RFM Analysis

RFM analysis evaluates customer behavior using three dimensions:

- Recency: the number of days since the customer's most recent purchase.
- Frequency: the number of distinct orders placed by the customer.
- Monetary: the total transaction value generated by the customer.

```{r rfm-analysis}
reference_date <- max(
  order_level$order_purchase_timestamp,
  na.rm = TRUE
) + days(1)

rfm_data <- order_level |>
  filter(
    !is.na(order_purchase_timestamp),
    !is.na(customer_unique_id)
  ) |>
  group_by(customer_unique_id) |>
  summarise(
    recency = as.numeric(
      difftime(
        reference_date,
        max(order_purchase_timestamp),
        units = "days"
      )
    ),
    frequency = n_distinct(order_id),
    monetary = sum(total_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

rfm_data <- rfm_data |>
  mutate(
    R_score = ntile(-recency, 5),
    F_score = ntile(frequency, 5),
    M_score = ntile(monetary, 5),
    RFM_score = R_score + F_score + M_score
  )

summary(rfm_data)
```

```{r rfm-visualization, fig.height=5}
ggplot(
  rfm_data,
  aes(frequency, monetary)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Customer Frequency vs Monetary Value",
    x = "Purchase Frequency",
    y = "Monetary Value"
  )
```

# 6. Predictive Modeling: Delivery Delay Classification

## 6.1 Target Definition

The objective is to predict whether an order experiences a delivery delay.

The target variable is defined as follows:

- `Late`: the actual delivery timestamp is later than the estimated delivery timestamp.
- `OnTime`: the actual delivery timestamp is equal to or earlier than the estimated delivery timestamp.

Only successfully delivered orders with both timestamps available are included.

```{r target-definition}
model_data <- order_level |>
  filter(
    order_status == "delivered",
    !is.na(order_delivered_customer_date),
    !is.na(order_estimated_delivery_date)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    is_late = factor(
      if_else(
        order_delivered_customer_date >
          order_estimated_delivery_date,
        "Late",
        "OnTime"
      ),
      levels = c("OnTime", "Late")
    )
  )

count(model_data, is_late)
```

## 6.2 Predictor Selection and Data Leakage Prevention

Predictors are selected from transaction and order characteristics that can reasonably be available before the final delivery outcome is known.

Actual delivery timestamps, carrier handover timestamps, actual delivery duration, delivery delay, and review information are excluded because they may introduce target leakage.

```{r predictor-selection}
model_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(
    customer_state = as.factor(customer_state),
    purchase_month = as.factor(purchase_month),
    purchase_weekday = as.factor(purchase_weekday)
  )

predictor_data <- model_data |>
  select(
    is_late,
    total_price,
    total_freight,
    item_count,
    avg_price,
    avg_freight,
    estimated_delivery_duration,
    approval_duration,
    avg_product_weight,
    avg_product_volume,
    product_categories,
    payment_value,
    payment_installments,
    payment_types,
    purchase_year,
    purchase_month,
    purchase_day,
    purchase_weekday,
    purchase_hour,
    is_weekend,
    customer_state
  )
```

## 6.3 Chronological Train-Test Split

The dataset is sorted by purchase timestamp before splitting. The earliest 80% of observations are used for training, while the most recent 20% are reserved for testing.

This approach simulates the practical scenario of predicting future orders using historical data.

```{r chronological-split}
model_data <- model_data |>
  arrange(order_purchase_timestamp)

predictor_data <- model_data |>
  select(
    is_late,
    total_price,
    total_freight,
    item_count,
    avg_price,
    avg_freight,
    estimated_delivery_duration,
    approval_duration,
    avg_product_weight,
    avg_product_volume,
    product_categories,
    payment_value,
    payment_installments,
    payment_types,
    purchase_year,
    purchase_month,
    purchase_day,
    purchase_weekday,
    purchase_hour,
    is_weekend,
    customer_state
  )

split_index <- floor(nrow(model_data) * 0.80)

train_data <- predictor_data[seq_len(split_index), ] |>
  droplevels()

test_data <- predictor_data[
  seq.int(split_index + 1, nrow(predictor_data)),
] |>
  droplevels()

count(train_data, is_late)
count(test_data, is_late)
```

## 6.4 Preprocessing and Model Training

The preprocessing workflow includes:

- Median imputation for numerical predictors.
- Mode imputation for categorical predictors.
- One-hot encoding for categorical variables.

Random Forest is used as the primary classification algorithm.

```{r model-training, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
rf_recipe <- recipe(
  is_late ~ .,
  data = train_data
) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

class_counts <- table(train_data$is_late)

class_weights <- length(train_data$is_late) /
  (length(class_counts) * class_counts)

rf_model <- rand_forest(
  trees = 300,
  min_n = 2
) |>
  set_engine(
    "ranger",
    importance = "permutation",
    class.weights = as.numeric(class_weights)
  ) |>
  set_mode("classification")

rf_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rf_recipe) |>
  add_model(rf_model)

rf_fit <- fit(
  rf_workflow,
  data = train_data
)

rf_fit
```

## 6.5 Baseline Model

A majority-class baseline is used to establish a simple reference performance. The Random Forest model should be evaluated against this baseline rather than being assessed in isolation.

```{r baseline-model}
majority_class <- names(
  which.max(table(train_data$is_late))
)

baseline_predictions <- factor(
  rep(majority_class, nrow(test_data)),
  levels = levels(test_data$is_late)
)

baseline_results <- tibble(
  truth = test_data$is_late,
  estimate = baseline_predictions
)

baseline_metrics <- tibble(
  metric = c("Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1-score"),
  value = c(
    accuracy_vec(
      baseline_results$truth,
      baseline_results$estimate
    ),
    precision_vec(
      baseline_results$truth,
      baseline_results$estimate,
      event_level = "second"
    ),
    recall_vec(
      baseline_results$truth,
      baseline_results$estimate,
      event_level = "second"
    ),
    f_meas_vec(
      baseline_results$truth,
      baseline_results$estimate,
      event_level = "second"
    )
  )
)

knitr::kable(baseline_metrics, digits = 4)
```

## 6.6 Model Evaluation

```{r model-predictions}
rf_probabilities <- predict(
  rf_fit,
  new_data = test_data,
  type = "prob"
)

rf_classes <- predict(
  rf_fit,
  new_data = test_data,
  type = "class"
)

rf_predictions <- bind_cols(
  tibble(truth = test_data$is_late),
  rf_classes,
  rf_probabilities
)

head(rf_predictions)
```

### Classification Metrics

```{r classification-metrics}
classification_metrics <- bind_rows(
  accuracy(rf_predictions, truth, .pred_class),
  precision(
    rf_predictions,
    truth,
    .pred_class,
    event_level = "second"
  ),
  recall(
    rf_predictions,
    truth,
    .pred_class,
    event_level = "second"
  ),
  f_meas(
    rf_predictions,
    truth,
    .pred_class,
    event_level = "second"
  )
)

roc_auc_result <- roc_auc(
  rf_predictions,
  truth,
  .pred_Late,
  event_level = "second"
)

pr_auc_result <- pr_auc(
  rf_predictions,
  truth,
  .pred_Late,
  event_level = "second"
)

classification_metrics
roc_auc_result
pr_auc_result
```

## 6.7 Confusion Matrix

The confusion matrix provides a detailed view of correct and incorrect predictions for both classes.

```{r confusion-matrix}
conf_mat(
  rf_predictions,
  truth = truth,
  estimate = .pred_class
)
```

## 6.8 ROC Curve and Precision-Recall Curve

```{r roc-curve, fig.height=5}
roc_curve(
  rf_predictions,
  truth,
  .pred_Late,
  event_level = "second"
) |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(title = "ROC Curve - Random Forest")
```

```{r pr-curve, fig.height=5}
pr_curve(
  rf_predictions,
  truth,
  .pred_Late,
  event_level = "second"
) |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(title = "Precision-Recall Curve - Random Forest")
```

## 6.9 Threshold Analysis

The classification threshold determines the minimum predicted probability required to classify an order as late.

A lower threshold generally increases recall but may reduce precision by generating more false positive predictions.

```{r threshold-analysis}
thresholds <- c(
  0.20, 0.30, 0.40,
  0.50, 0.60, 0.70
)

threshold_results <- purrr::map_dfr(
  thresholds,
  function(threshold) {
    predicted_class <- factor(
      if_else(
        rf_predictions$.pred_Late >= threshold,
        "Late",
        "OnTime"
      ),
      levels = c("OnTime", "Late")
    )

    tibble(
      truth = rf_predictions$truth,
      estimate = predicted_class
    ) |>
      summarise(
        threshold = threshold,
        precision = precision_vec(
          truth,
          estimate,
          event_level = "second"
        ),
        recall = recall_vec(
          truth,
          estimate,
          event_level = "second"
        ),
        f1 = f_meas_vec(
          truth,
          estimate,
          event_level = "second"
        )
      )
  }
)

knitr::kable(threshold_results, digits = 4)
```

```{r threshold-visualization, fig.height=5}
threshold_results |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(precision, recall, f1),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "score"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(threshold, score, color = metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Performance Across Classification Thresholds",
    x = "Classification Threshold",
    y = "Score",
    color = "Metric"
  )
```

## 6.10 Feature Importance

Permutation importance is used to evaluate how much model performance decreases when the values of a predictor are randomly shuffled.

```{r feature-importance}
importance_values <- ranger::importance(
  extract_fit_parsnip(rf_fit)$fit
)

importance_data <- tibble(
  feature = names(importance_values),
  importance = as.numeric(importance_values)
) |>
  arrange(desc(importance)) |>
  slice_head(n = 15)

knitr::kable(importance_data, digits = 4)
```

```{r feature-importance-plot, fig.height=6}
ggplot(
  importance_data,
  aes(
    x = reorder(feature, importance),
    y = importance
  )
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 15 Feature Importance",
    x = "Feature",
    y = "Permutation Importance"
  )
```

# 7. Conclusion and Further Work

## 7.1 Conclusion

This project presents an end-to-end analysis of the Olist Brazilian E-Commerce dataset.

The main analytical stages include:

1. Data understanding and quality assessment.
2. Data preprocessing and feature engineering.
3. Exploratory data analysis.
4. Statistical hypothesis testing using the Mann-Whitney U test.
5. Customer segmentation using RFM analysis.
6. Delivery delay classification using Random Forest.
7. Model evaluation, threshold analysis, and feature importance.

Quantitative conclusions should be based on the actual outputs generated by the analysis. Descriptive patterns should not automatically be interpreted as causal relationships.

## 7.2 Limitations

Several limitations should be considered:

- The dataset represents historical transactions and may not reflect current operational conditions.
- The classification task only includes successfully delivered orders with available actual and estimated delivery timestamps.
- The available variables may not fully represent operational logistics conditions.
- Temporal distribution shifts may affect the generalization performance of the model.
- Feature importance measures predictive contribution rather than causal influence.
